chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sent his sacrificial animal (hady) with a group of people who were driving it, and he appointed a day for them to put the halter on their sacrificial animal and enter the state of ihram. He said: 'It becomes obligatory upon him to observe what is obligatory upon the one in ihram on the day he appointed for them, until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination.' I said: 'What if you saw that they differed regarding the appointed time and delayed in the journey for him, and he needs to exit the state of ihram on the day he appointed for them?' He said: 'There is no blame upon him if he exits the state of ihram on the day he appointed for them.'

key_terms.هَدْي: Sacrificial animal sent for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.يَحِلَّ: To exit the state of ihram
key_terms.يُحْرِمُونَ: They enter the state of ihram (sacred ritual state)
key_terms.يُقَلِّدُونَ: They put the halter on (signifying the start of ihram ritual)

ai.seo_question: When does a person become bound by ihram rules if they send their Hajj sacrifice with others?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the ruling for a Hajj pilgrim who dispatches their sacrificial animal (*hady*) with companions, establishing that the sender assumes the legal status of *muhrim* from the agreed-upon day until the animal arrives. The Imam provides a practical concession: if the companions delay or the journey is protracted, the sender is not held accountable for remaining in ihram indefinitely and may exit the state on the appointed day without blame. This highlights the Shia juristic principle of ease (*taysir*) in ritual obligations when external circumstances beyond one's control cause delay.
